paragraphs.en: In the 1420s, the governor of Samarkand did something unusual for a ruler: he built a scientific institution. Mirzo Ulugh Beg, the grandson of Amir Temur, was more interested in the stars than in war. On a hill outside the city, he constructed an observatory that was one of the most advanced in the world at that time.

The heart of the building was an enormous instrument, a curved structure cut partly into the rock, with a radius of around forty metres. Using it, astronomers could measure the position of the Sun and other celestial bodies with remarkable accuracy. Because there were no telescopes yet, size was the key to precision: the bigger the instrument, the smaller the errors.

The most famous result of this work was a star catalogue listing the positions of about a thousand stars. It was the most accurate star catalogue made since ancient times, and scholars continued to study it for centuries. Ulugh Beg and his team also calculated the length of the year with an error of only about a minute.

Sadly, the observatory did not survive its creator for long. After Ulugh Beg was killed in 1449, the building was abandoned and gradually destroyed. For more than four centuries, its exact location was forgotten.

In 1908, the archaeologist Vasily Vyatkin found the remains of the great instrument underground. Today, visitors to Samarkand can walk down into the surviving part of it and visit a small museum nearby, which tells the story of a ruler who chose science.
